name: Sacred history
plain_explanation: The idea that history is not just a record of events but a story with a beginning (Creation), a meaning, and a future goal, in which God's purposes are worked out through a particular people.
precise_definition: A providential narrative of history, beginning with the Creation and moving toward a future consummation, that justifies 'the ways of God to man' and treats historical events as episodes in a divine plan.
why_it_mattered: It gave Christianity (and, in Russell's view, the Jewish tradition it inherited) a linear, purposeful view of time in place of the cyclical views common in Greek and other ancient thought, and it made suffering and defeat interpretable rather than meaningless.
historical_origin: Developed and crystallized among the Jews, especially during and after the Babylonian captivity, as they reinterpreted their national catastrophes as part of a coherent divine story.
examples: The Old Testament narrative from Creation through the Exile and return
Apocalyptic literature such as the Book of Enoch projecting sacred history into the future (New Jerusalem, resurrection, Messiah)
competing_positions: Greek/Platonic view that the truly real is timeless and unchanging, so that temporal history as such has no ultimate metaphysical significance
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell later argues (in his discussion of Saint Augustine's City of God) that this Jewish pattern of sacred history was adapted wholesale by Christianity and, in secularized form, even structures modern political eschatologies such as Marxism.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious and political: it explained why a small, often-conquered nation still believed itself central to a cosmic plan.

evolution.treatment: The idea that history is not just a record of events but a story with a beginning (Creation), a meaning, and a future goal, in which God's purposes are worked out through a particular people.
